The night train slid into the station with a whisper of steel and a breath of rust, its long wheels catching the platform in a slow, almost silent arrival. I had left this town as a child, and now, decades later, the tracks that once carried me away were carrying me back, though I no longer recognized the faces of the windows or the smell of the platform. The station was empty, its lamps dim, its benches cold, and the only sound was the distant hum of the engine as it stopped, as it always did, at a place that had once held my name. I did not speak; I did not look; I only waited, and the night train waited with me.

Outside the station, the town lay in a blue dusk, its streets folded into the quiet of the hour, its houses dark and shut, their windows like black eyes on the hour. I walked from the platform to the road, and the road remembered me, though I did not remember it.
